title: 29  Model Evaluation - Review Questions
text:
This notebook contains review questions for lectures/050_evaluation.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

29.0.1 Question 1
For a fixed regression function \(f\) and fresh data \(D=\{(X_n,Y_n)\}_{n=1}^M\sim P^M\), the lecture defines \[
\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D,f)=\frac1M\sum_{n=1}^M (Y_n-f(X_n))^2.
\] Show that \[\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb E_D[\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D,f)\mid f] = E_{(X,Y)\sim P}[(Y-f(X))^2]
\] for a new generic draw \((X,Y)\sim P\).


Answer

Since \(f\) is fixed under the conditional expectation, \[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb E\left[\frac1M\sum_{n=1}^M (Y_n-f(X_n))^2\right]
=\frac1M\sum_{n=1}^M \mathbb E[(Y_n-f(X_n))^2].
\] The i.i.d. assumption gives each summand the same distribution as \((Y-f(X))^2\), so \[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)\sim P}[(Y-f(X))^2].
\]



29.0.2 Question 2
For a fixed classifier \(f\), let
\[
\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D,f)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n=1}^M \mathbf{1}\{f(X_n)\ne Y_n\}.
\]
Express \(\mathrm{Perf}(f)\) as a probability.
Hint: \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{A\}]\).


Answer

The quantity \(\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D,f)\) is the average classification error on the evaluation dataset \(D\). Each indicator \(\mathbf{1}\{f(X_n)\ne Y_n\}\) equals 1 if the classifier makes a mistake on observation \(n\), and equals 0 otherwise.
Since \(f\) is fixed, the only randomness comes from the evaluation data. The true performance is the expected value of this evaluation error on fresh data:
\[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb{E}_D[\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D,f)].
\]
Substituting the definition of \(\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D,f)\) gives
\[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb{E}_D\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n=1}^M \mathbf{1}\{f(X_n)\ne Y_n\}\right].
\]
By linearity of expectation,
\[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n=1}^M \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}\{f(X_n)\ne Y_n\}\right].
\]
Because the observations are drawn from the same distribution, each term in the average is the probability that \(f\) makes a mistake on a fresh observation. Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P}[\mathbf{1}\{f(X)\ne Y\}].
\]
Using the identity \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{A\}]\), we can write this as
\[
\mathrm{Perf}(f)=\mathbb{P}_{(X,Y)\sim P}(f(X)\ne Y).
\]
So the true performance of a fixed classifier is the probability that it misclassifies a fresh draw from the data-generating distribution.



29.0.3 Question 3
The lecture says \(D_{eval}\perp D_{train}\) is sufficient for \(D_{eval}\perp\hat f\) when \(\hat f=A(D_{train})\). Why?


Answer

A standard property of independence says that if \(U\perp V\), then \(U\perp g(V)\) for every function \(g\). Taking \(U=D_{eval}\), \(V=D_{train}\), and \(g=A\) gives \(D_{eval}\perp A(D_{train})=\hat f\).



29.0.4 Question 4
Construct a concrete edge case, matching the lecture’s discussion, where \(D_{eval}=D_{train}\) but nevertheless \(D_{eval}\perp\hat f\).


Answer

Let \(A(D)\) ignore its input and always return the constant model \(\hat f(x)=0\). Then \(\hat f\) is deterministic, so it is independent of every random variable, including \(D_{eval}=D_{train}\). Hence \(D_{eval}\perp\hat f\) even though \(D_{eval}\) and \(D_{train}\) are identical. This illustrates that independence from the fitted model is the key condition, not literal separation from the training set by itself.



29.0.5 Question 5
For least squares regression with noise variance \(\sigma^2\), the lecture states the optimism formula \[
\mathbb E[\mathrm{Perf}(\hat f)-\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{train},\hat f)]
=\frac{2\sigma^2}{N}d.
\] Compute the optimism when \(N=100\), \(d=8\), and \(\sigma^2=4\). Interpret the units of the answer.


Answer

Substitution gives \[
\frac{2\sigma^2}{N}d=\frac{2\cdot 4}{100}\cdot 8=\frac{64}{100}=0.64.
\] Since the metric is mean squared error, the optimism is measured in squared-response units. It says the expected training MSE is lower than the corresponding fresh-data MSE by \(0.64\).



29.0.6 Question 6
Use the covariance version of Efron’s optimism theorem to explain precisely why no optimism appears when every fitted prediction \(\hat y_i\) is independent of its observed response \(y_i\).


Answer

If \(\hat y_i\perp y_i\) and both variables have finite second moments, then \[
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\mathbb E[\hat y_i y_i]-\mathbb E[\hat y_i]\mathbb E[y_i]=0.
\] Therefore \[
\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=0.
\] Under the theorem’s assumptions, the expected gap between true performance and training performance is then \(0\).



29.0.7 Question 7
Assume that \(y\) and \(\hat y\) are vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^N\), with
\[
\hat y = Sy,
\]
where \(S\) is a fixed \(N\times N\) matrix. Also assume
\[
y_i=\mu_i+\varepsilon_i,
\]
where the errors \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent, have mean 0, and have variance \(\sigma^2\).
Show that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\sigma^2\mathrm{tr}(S).
\]


Answer

Since \(\hat y=Sy\), the \(i\)th fitted value is
\[
\hat y_i=\sum_{j=1}^N S_{ij}y_j.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\mathrm{Cov}\left(\sum_{j=1}^N S_{ij}y_j,y_i\right).
\]
Because covariance is linear in its first argument and the entries of \(S\) are fixed constants,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\sum_{j=1}^N S_{ij}\mathrm{Cov}(y_j,y_i).
\]
Now use the model \(y_i=\mu_i+\varepsilon_i\). The mean terms \(\mu_i\) are fixed, so they do not affect covariance. Thus,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(y_j,y_i)=\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_j,\varepsilon_i).
\]
Because the errors are independent and each has variance \(\sigma^2\),
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(y_j,y_i)=
\begin{cases}
\sigma^2, & j=i,\\
0, & j\ne i.
\end{cases}
\]
So in the sum
\[
\sum_{j=1}^N S_{ij}\mathrm{Cov}(y_j,y_i),
\]
all terms are zero except the term with \(j=i\). Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=S_{ii}\sigma^2.
\]
Finally, summing over \(i\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\sum_{i=1}^N S_{ii}\sigma^2.
\]
Since \(\sigma^2\) is constant,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^N S_{ii}.
\]
By definition, the trace of \(S\) is the sum of its diagonal entries:
\[
\mathrm{tr}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^N S_{ii}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N \mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)=\sigma^2\mathrm{tr}(S).
\]



29.0.8 Question 8
A model-selection procedure chooses polynomial the degree \(\hat r\) with the smallest evaluation MSE on a fixed evaluation set, then reports that same minimum as the performance estimate. Identify the independence condition from the lecture that is broken, and describe the expected direction of the bias.


Answer

After selecting \(\hat r\) using the evaluation set, the final chosen model or procedure depends on \(D_{eval}\). Therefore \(D_{eval}\perp\hat f\) no longer holds for the selected model. The reported minimum evaluation error is typically optimistic: among several noisy estimates, selecting the smallest tends to underestimate the fresh-data error of the selected degree.



29.0.9 Question 9
Cross-validation estimates algorithm-level performance rather than the performance of one fixed model. Write the target quantity for an algorithm \(A\) trained on \(n\) observations, and explain why \(k\)-fold CV more directly targets \(n=N(k-1)/k\) than \(n=N\).


Answer

The algorithm-level target for training size \(n\) is \[
\mathbb E_{D_{train}\sim P^n}[\mathrm{Perf}(A(D_{train}))].
\] In each \(k\)-fold CV fit, the algorithm is trained on \(N(k-1)/k\) observations, not all \(N\). Therefore the models being evaluated are draws from the distribution of \(A(D_{train})\) with training size \(N(k-1)/k\). The final model trained on all \(N\) observations may perform slightly better, which is why the lecture describes CV as somewhat pessimistic.



29.0.10 Question 10
A collaborator asks which of the \(k\) fitted models from cross-validation should be deployed. What’s the answer?


Answer

None of the fold-specific models \(\hat f^{(j)}=A(D\setminus D_j)\) is the deployed model. They are auxiliary models used to estimate the performance of the training procedure. After choosing the procedure \(A\) and estimating its performance, one trains \[
\hat f_{final}=A(D_{all})
\] on all available data and deploys that model. The CV score is interpreted as evidence about the procedure’s expected fresh-data performance, not as the fresh-data performance of one particular fold model.



29.0.11 Question 11
Resampling by repeated random splits produces \[
R_B=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B \hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{eval}^{(b)},\hat f^{(b)}).
\] Assuming the random splits are independent, compute \(\mathrm{Var}(R_B)\) in terms of the variance of one split score \(S_b = \hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{eval}^{(b)},\hat f^{(b)})\) assuming that the \(S_b\) are independent with common variance \(\mathrm{Var}(S_b) = \tau^2\).


Answer

If the split scores \(S_b=\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{eval}^{(b)},\hat f^{(b)})\) are independent conditional on the dataset and each has variance \(\tau^2\), then \[
\mathrm{Var}(R_B)=\mathrm{Var}\left(\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B S_b\right)
=\frac1{B^2}\sum_{b=1}^B\mathrm{Var}(S_b)
=\frac{\tau^2}{B}.
\] (Note that real split scores are often dependent because they reuse observations.)



29.0.12 Question 12
For a binary classifier, suppose the evaluation set gives \(TP=40\), \(FP=10\), \(FN=20\), and \(TN=30\). Compute classification error and F1 score. Which one uses \(TN\) directly?


Answer

The evaluation size is \(M=40+10+20+30=100\). Classification error is \[
\frac{FP+FN}{M}=\frac{10+20}{100}=0.30.
\] The F1 score is \[
\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}=\frac{80}{80+10+20}=\frac{80}{110}=\frac{8}{11}\approx 0.727.
\]



29.0.13 Question 13
Suppose we evaluate two classifiers, A and B, on the same dataset of 100 observations. The dataset has 10 positive cases and 90 negative cases.
The confusion matrices are:



Classifier
TP
FP
FN
TN




A
0
0
10
90


B
8
20
2
70



For each classifier, calculate:

The classification error.
The F1 score.

Then answer the following:

Which classifier is better according to classification error?
Which classifier is better according to F1 score?
Briefly explain what this example shows about metric choice.



Answer

For classifier A,
\[
\text{Error}_A = \frac{0 + 10}{100} = 0.10
\]
and
\[
F1_A = \frac{2(0)}{2(0) + 0 + 10} = 0.
\]
For classifier B,
\[
\text{Error}_B = \frac{20 + 2}{100} = 0.22
\]
and
\[
F1_B = \frac{2(8)}{2(8) + 20 + 2}
= \frac{16}{38}
\approx 0.421.
\]
Classifier A is better by classification error because (0.10 < 0.22).
Classifier B is better by F1 score because (0.421 > 0).
So the two metrics rank the classifiers in opposite orders. This shows that the choice of evaluation metric can change which model appears better.



29.0.14 Question 14
A dataset is randomly split into \(D_{train}\) and \(D_{eval}\), but preprocessing parameters such as centering and scaling are fit using all observations before the split. Does the lecture’s independence requirement automatically hold? Give a precise answer.


Answer

No. If preprocessing parameters are estimated from all observations and then used by the training algorithm, the fitted model can depend on information from \(D_{eval}\). Then \(D_{eval}\perp\hat f\) need not hold, even if the raw rows were randomly split. To preserve the fresh-data interpretation, preprocessing parameters that affect the model must be fit using only \(D_{train}\) within each split or fold, then applied to the corresponding evaluation data.



29.0.15 Question 15
A false proof claims: “Because each cross-validation evaluation fold \(D_j\) was not used to train \(\hat f^{(j)}\), the \(k\) fold scores are independent random variables.” Identify the false step and give the correct dependence issue.


Answer

The false step is confusing independence of a fold from its own fitted model with independence among the fold scores. The training sets \(D\setminus D_j\) overlap heavily across folds, and the fold scores are all functions of the same original dataset \(D\). Therefore the scores are generally dependent. Cross-validation can still be useful, but the simple variance formula for an average of independent fold scores is not automatically valid.



29.0.16 Question 16
The following statement is missing an important assumption:
“If \(D_{eval}\) is independent of \(\hat f\), then \(\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{eval},\hat f)\) estimates \(\mathrm{Perf}(\hat f)\).”
What assumption is missing?


Answer

The missing assumption is that the evaluation data must come from the same distribution used to define fresh-data performance. In other words, we need
\[
D_{eval}\sim P^M.
\]
Independence alone only says that the evaluation data were not used to train the model. That helps prevent data reuse or overfitting to the evaluation set. But it does not guarantee that the evaluation set represents the target population we care about.
An important idea is training/testing dataset drift. A test set can be independent of the fitted model and still give the wrong answer if it comes from a different distribution than the fresh data we care about. In that case, the evaluation error estimates performance on the test distribution, not performance on the target distribution \(P\)



29.0.17 Question 17
In the lecture’s cartoon plot of training error and testing error versus model complexity, divide the horizontal axis into three qualitative regions: low complexity, intermediate complexity, and high complexity. For each region, state whether the main problem is underfitting, reasonable generalization, or overfitting, and describe the typical relationship between training error and testing error.


Answer

At low complexity, the model class is too restricted to capture the signal, so both training error and testing error are relatively high. This is underfitting: the model is not fitting either the observed data or new data very well.
At intermediate complexity, the model has enough flexibility to capture much of the real signal without adapting too strongly to sample-specific noise. Training error is lower than in the low-complexity region, and testing error is typically near its minimum. The train-test gap may exist, but it is not yet large.
At high complexity, training error keeps decreasing, sometimes nearly to zero, but testing error increases. This is overfitting: the model is fitting noise or accidental patterns in \(D_{train}\) that do not repeat in fresh data.



29.0.18 Question 18
A student looks at the complexity plot and says: “If increasing model complexity always lowers training error, then the most complex model must be the best model.” Diagnose the mistake using the lecture’s distinction between performance on \(D_{train}\) and performance on new independent data.


Answer

The mistake is treating training error as the target quantity. Training error measures how well \(\hat f\) fits the same data used to construct it, so it is affected by the dependence between \(D_{train}\) and \(\hat f\). It can keep improving as complexity increases because the model has more ways to adapt to this particular dataset.
The lecture’s target is performance on new independent data, represented by \(\mathrm{Perf}(\hat f)\) or by evaluation error on \(D_{eval}\) satisfying \(D_{eval}\sim P^M\) and \(D_{eval}\perp \hat f\). A highly complex model may lower training error by fitting sample-specific quirks, but those quirks do not generalize. Therefore the most complex model can have worse testing error even though it has better training error.



29.0.19 Question 20
Two polynomial degrees have nearly the same evaluation error on an independent evaluation set. Degree 4 has noticeably higher training error, while degree 14 has much lower training error. Based on the lecture’s discussion of complexity and overfitting, what would be a reasonable reason to prefer degree 4?


Answer

If the independent evaluation errors are essentially tied, then the observed advantage of degree 14 is only on the training data. That advantage is less trustworthy because training error is optimistic: the degree-14 model has more capacity to adapt to noise and sample-specific quirks in \(D_{train}\).
A reasonable reason to prefer degree 4 is that it achieves comparable estimated fresh-data performance with less dependence on the particular training sample. The argument is not that lower complexity is automatically better; it is that, when independent evaluation performance is similar, the extra training-fit improvement from the more complex model is weak evidence of better generalization and stronger evidence of possible overfitting.



29.0.20 Question 21
The lecture says complex models are more sensitive to the data. Translate this sensitivity statement into the language of Efron’s optimism discussion: what tends to happen to the covariance terms \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)\) as the fitted model adapts more strongly to \(D_{train}\)? How does that relate to the widening gap between training and testing error in the complexity diagram?


Answer

When a fitted model adapts strongly to \(D_{train}\), each fitted value \(\hat y_i\) tends to depend more strongly on the observed response \(y_i\). In Efron’s optimism formula, that stronger dependence appears as larger positive covariance terms \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat y_i,y_i)\).
Larger covariance terms imply larger optimism: the training error is expected to be farther below the fresh-data error. This is the same phenomenon shown in the high-complexity part of the cartoon diagram, where the training curve continues downward while the testing curve turns upward and the train-test gap widens.

title: 30  Model Selection - Review Questions
text:
This notebook contains review questions for lectures/060_model_selection.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

30.0.1 Question 1
For a fixed learning algorithm \(A\), we train \[
\hat f = A(D_{train})
\] and evaluate performance on an independent evaluation set \(D_{eval}\). What changes when we move from a fixed algorithm \(A\) to fitting over a family \(\{A_\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda\}\) and choosing the best candidate?


Answer

For a fixed algorithm \(A\), the evaluation set is independent of the fitted model \(\hat f=A(D_{train})\), so the evaluation error estimates performance on new data.
In model selection, each fixed candidate \(\hat f_\lambda\) can still be evaluated on \(D_{val}\) because \(\hat f_\lambda\) was trained only on \(D_{train}\). The problem arises when we choose \[
\hat\lambda=\arg\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda}e_\lambda.
\]
Now \(\hat\lambda\) depends on \(D_{val}\). Therefore the selected model, \(\hat f_{\hat\lambda}\), also depends on \(D_{val}\). The validation set has become part of the model-building procedure, not just an independent evaluation set.
As a result, the selected validation error \(e_{\hat\lambda}\) is typically optimistically biased. It is the minimum of several noisy estimates, so it tends to make the selected model look better than it really is. To estimate final performance honestly, we need a separate test set that was not used for either fitting or selecting \(\lambda\).



30.0.2 Question 2
For three candidate polynomial degrees (\(\lambda\)), the validation MSEs \(e_\lambda\) are



\(\lambda\)
1
3
5




\(e_\lambda\)
4.8
2.1
2.7



Using the lecture’s loss-minimization rule, compute \(\hat\lambda\).


Answer

The selected degree is \[
\hat\lambda=\arg\min_{\lambda\in\{1,3,5\}}e_\lambda=3,
\] because \(2.1\) is the smallest validation MSE.



30.0.3 Question 3
For a fixed \(\lambda\), why can \(\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{val},\hat f_\lambda)\) still be a valid estimate of that candidate’s performance, even though the selected validation error \(\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{val},\hat f_{\hat\lambda})\) is typically optimistic?


Answer

For a fixed \(\lambda\), the model \(\hat f_\lambda=A_\lambda(D_{train})\) is trained without using \(D_{val}\). If \(D_{val}\) is an independent sample from the target distribution, then \(D_{val}\perp \hat f_\lambda\), so validation performance estimates fresh-data performance for that fixed candidate.
After selection, however, \(\hat\lambda\) is chosen because it performed well on \(D_{val}\). The reported selected validation error is no longer the error of a candidate fixed in advance; it is the minimum over several noisy validation estimates. This selection step creates dependence between \(D_{val}\) and the final chosen model, making the selected validation error optimistic.



30.0.4 Question 4
The lecture says the difference between tuning weights \(w\) inside an algorithm and choosing a hyperparameter \(\lambda\) is less important than it may seem. Why? Give a reason in terms of the final model-building procedure.


Answer

Both operations are data-dependent choices that affect the final fitted model. Tuning weights \(w\) uses training data to choose parameters within a model class. Choosing \(\lambda\) uses validation or cross-validation data to choose among model classes, complexities, or training rules. In both cases, the output is a function of data.
The relevant object is therefore the whole pipeline \(\mathcal P(D)\), not just an isolated algorithm call. If the pipeline uses data to choose \(w\), \(\lambda\), preprocessing choices, or model classes, those choices are part of the learning procedure that produced \(\hat f\).



30.0.5 Question 5
In a three-way split, assign each dataset to its role: \(D_{train}\), \(D_{val}\), and \(D_{test}\). For each one, state whether it is allowed to influence the fitted candidate models, the selected \(\hat\lambda\), and the final reported performance estimate.


Answer

\(D_{train}\) is used to fit candidate models \(\hat f_\lambda=A_\lambda(D_{train})\). It influences fitted candidate models, but it should not be used as the final performance estimate.
\(D_{val}\) is used to choose \(\hat\lambda\) by comparing candidate validation errors. It influences the selected model through \(\hat\lambda\), so it is part of model building and should not be used as the final unbiased evaluation set.
\(D_{test}\) is held out until the end. It should not influence candidate fitting or \(\hat\lambda\). Its role is to provide the final reported estimate \(\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{test},\hat f)\).



30.0.6 Question 5
A colleague trains several models, chooses the one with the smallest test error, and then reports that same test error as the final performance estimate. Diagnose a potential problem with this logic.


Answer

The flaw is that the test set has been used for model selection. Once test performance determines which model is chosen, the test set is no longer a pure final evaluation set; it has become validation data. The final selected model depends on the test set through the choice of model.



30.0.7 Question 6
Why should we evaluate on \(D_{test}\) only once, at the end? What would happen if the analyst repeatedly used \(D_{test}\) to make decisions.


Answer

The test set is useful for final evaluation only if it remains independent of the final model-building procedure. If the analyst repeatedly checks test performance and changes models, hyperparameters, preprocessing, or features in response, then the final model depends on the test set. It no longer provides an independent estimate of fresh-data performance, and the final reported test error can become optimistically biased.



30.0.8 Question 7
True or False: Since the validation set \(D_{val}\) was not used to fit any individual candidate model \(\hat f_\lambda\), it is independent of the final selected model \(\hat f_{\hat\lambda}\).


Answer

False.
It is true that, for each fixed \(\lambda\), the candidate model \[
\hat f_\lambda=A_\lambda(D_{train})
\] was fit without using \(D_{val}\).
The false step is concluding that \(D_{val}\) is therefore independent of the final selected model. The validation set is used to choose \[
\hat\lambda=\arg\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\hat{\mathrm{Perf}}(D_{val},\hat f_\lambda).
\]
So \(\hat\lambda\) depends on \(D_{val}\). Since the final selected model is \(\hat f_{\hat\lambda}\), the final model can also depend on \(D_{val}\), even though no individual candidate was directly fit using \(D_{val}\).



30.0.9 Question 8
The lecture says selection bias is worse when \(\Lambda\) is large or searched aggressively. Why?


Answer

Each validation score \(e_\lambda\) is a noisy estimate of the corresponding candidate’s true fresh-data performance. When the procedure chooses \(\hat\lambda\) by minimizing \(e_\lambda\), it tends to pick a candidate whose validation estimate is low partly because of genuine performance and partly because of favorable noise. As \(\Lambda\) grows or the search becomes more aggressive, there are more noisy estimates from which to choose. The minimum of many noisy estimates is more likely to be unusually low, so the selected validation error becomes more optimistic.



30.0.10 Question 9
For two candidates \(\lambda=1,2\), suppose their true performances are equal to \(1\), but their validation errors are \[
e_1=1+\varepsilon_1,\qquad e_2=1+\varepsilon_2,
\] where \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) are independent and take values \(-0.2\) and \(0.2\) with probability \(1/2\) each. Compute \(\mathbb E[\min(e_1,e_2)]\) and compare it with the true performance \(1\).


Answer

The possible pairs of errors are equally likely:

\((-0.2,-0.2)\) gives \(\min(e_1,e_2)=0.8\).
\((-0.2,0.2)\) gives \(\min(e_1,e_2)=0.8\).
\((0.2,-0.2)\) gives \(\min(e_1,e_2)=0.8\).
\((0.2,0.2)\) gives \(\min(e_1,e_2)=1.2\).

Therefore \[
\mathbb E[\min(e_1,e_2)]
=\frac14(0.8+0.8+0.8+1.2)=0.9.
\] Even though both candidates have true performance \(1\) and error distributed symmetrically around zero, the expected selected validation error is \(0.9\), which is optimistically low.



30.0.11 Question 10
Suppose we are doing polynomial model selection. For each degree \(d\), let \(\hat f_d\) be the polynomial regression model of degree \(d\) fit on the training set \(D_{train}\). Let
\[
e_d=\hat{\mathrm{MSE}}(D_{val},\hat f_d)
\]
be the validation mean squared error for degree \(d\).
Now suppose we choose not only the polynomial degree, but also how large a degree-search space to allow. For a maximum allowed degree \(K\), define
\[
\hat d_K=\arg\min_{0\le d\le K} e_d.
\]
The selected validation error for this search space is
\[
e_{\hat d_K}=\min_{0\le d\le K} e_d.
\]
Show that the selected validation error \(e_{\hat d_K}\) is nonincreasing as \(K\) increases. In other words, explain why allowing yourself to search over degrees \(0,\dots,K+1\) cannot produce a larger selected validation error than searching only over degrees \(0,\dots,K\).


Answer

When \(K\) increases to \(K+1\), the search set expands from
\[
\{0,\dots,K\}
\]
to
\[
\{0,\dots,K,K+1\}.
\]
The old selected degree \(\hat d_K\) is still available in the larger search set. Therefore, the minimum over the larger set cannot be greater than the minimum over the smaller set:
\[
\min_{0\le d\le K+1} e_d
\le
\min_{0\le d\le K} e_d.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
e_{\hat d_{K+1}}\le e_{\hat d_K}.
\]
So the selected validation error is nonincreasing as \(K\) increases.
This does not mean that true test performance must improve as \(K\) increases. It only means that the best validation error found inside a larger search space cannot get worse, because the larger search space contains all the old options plus one additional degree.



30.0.12 Question 11
Does the monotonicity in Question 19 imply that test error of the selected model must also be nonincreasing in \(K\)?


Answer

No. The monotonicity applies to the selected validation error because the procedure explicitly minimizes validation error over an expanding set. Test error is not used in the selection rule. As \(K\) increases, the selected degree may change to one with lower validation error but higher test error.



30.0.13 Question 12
Nested cross-validation uses two loops: an inner loop and an outer loop. What is the purpose of each loop?


Answer

The inner loop is used for model selection. Within each outer training set, the inner cross-validation loop compares candidate models or hyperparameter values and chooses the one with the best inner validation performance.
The outer loop is used for performance estimation. In each outer split, the entire model-selection procedure is run using only the outer training data. The selected model is then evaluated on the outer test fold, which was not used for either fitting candidates or choosing hyperparameters.
Thus, the inner loop answers:

Which model or hyperparameter setting should we choose?

The outer loop answers:

How well does the full selection-and-fitting procedure perform on new data?




30.0.14 Question 13
In nested CV with \(N=120\) observations, \(k_{outer}=4\), and \(k_{inner}=3\), assume folds are equal size. For one outer fold, how many observations are in \(D_{test}^{(j)}\) and \(D_{train\text{-}val}^{(j)}\)? Inside that outer training set, how many observations are used to train each inner-fold candidate model?


Answer

With \(k_{outer}=4\), each outer test fold has \[
120/4=30
\] observations. The corresponding outer training-validation set has \[
120-30=90
\] observations.
Inside that set, \(k_{inner}=3\) means each inner validation fold has \(90/3=30\) observations, so each inner candidate model is trained on \[
90-30=60
\] observations.



30.0.15 Question 14
A data scientist claims: “Nested CV estimates the performance of the exact final model I will train using all \(N\) observations in the data set.” Is this true?


Answer

The claim is not quite correct. Nested CV estimates the performance of the full model-selection procedure, when that procedure is applied to training samples of the outer-training size. Each outer fold runs the entire inner selection procedure on \(D\setminus D_j\) and evaluates the resulting model on \(D_j\). The outer average is therefore evidence about the procedure’s expected fresh-data performance, not the exact conditional performance of the one final model later trained on all \(N\) observations.



30.0.16 Question 15
Why is it reasonable, after choosing \(\hat\lambda\) using \(D_{val}\), to retrain the final model on \(D_{train}\cup D_{val}\) before evaluating on \(D_{test}\)?


Answer

After \(\hat\lambda\) has been chosen, \(D_{val}\) has already served its role in model building. Retraining on \(D_{train}\cup D_{val}\) uses more non-test data to fit the final model, which can improve the final model because it has more training observations. This does not invalidate the final test evaluation as long as \(D_{test}\) remains untouched by training and selection.



30.0.17 Question 16
An analyst has a dataset and wants to train and evaluate a predictive model. Before splitting the data into training, validation, and test sets, the analyst selects the top 20 features by computing each feature’s correlation with the response using all observations. The analyst then splits the data, trains several candidate models using the selected features, chooses among them using validation error, and reports the final test error.
Does data leakage occur in this pipeline?


Answer

The leakage occurs during feature selection.
The test set improperly influences the preprocessing step, because the top 20 features were selected using all observations, including observations from \(D_{test}\). Feature selection is part of the model-building pipeline, so information from the test set has entered the construction of the final model. As a result, the final model depends on \(D_{test}\) even though the model was not directly fit on \(D_{test}\). The test set is no longer independent of the final model, so the reported test error can be optimistically biased.



30.0.18 Question 17
Compare a validation set and a test set in one sentence each, using the criterion “is this data allowed to affect the final model?” Then explain why the names matter less than the role the data actually plays.


Answer

A validation set is allowed to affect the final model through choices such as \(\hat\lambda\), model class, preprocessing, or feature selection. A test set is not allowed to affect the final model; it is reserved for final performance estimation. The names matter less than the role because a dataset called “test” becomes validation data if it is used to choose among models. Conversely, a dataset functions as a test set only if it remains unused until the final evaluation.

title: 31  K-Nearest Neighbors - Review Questions
text:
This notebook contains review questions for lectures/070_knn.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

31.0.1 Question 1
The lecture begins with the risk \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)\sim P}[\ell(Y,s(X))].
\] What is the target \(s^*\) trying to find?


Answer

The target is \[
s^*=\arg\min_s R(s),
\] the score function with smallest expected loss under the true data-generating distribution \(P\).



31.0.2 Question 2
Starting from \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)}[\ell(Y,s(X))],
\] use the law of total expectation to derive the conditional-risk form \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_X[L_X(s(X))],
\qquad
L_x(t)=\mathbb E[\ell(Y,t)\mid X=x].
\]


Answer

By the law of total expectation, \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_X\left[\mathbb E[\ell(Y,s(X))\mid X]\right].
\] After conditioning on \(X=x\), the value \(s(X)\) becomes \(s(x)\), so the inner expectation is \[
\mathbb E[\ell(Y,s(x))\mid X=x].
\] Defining \[
L_x(t)=\mathbb E[\ell(Y,t)\mid X=x]
\] gives \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_X[L_X(s(X))].
\]



31.0.3 Question 3
The lecture says unrestricted risk minimization can be done pointwise. Why are we free to choosen each value of \(s(x)\) separately for each value of \(x\)?


Answer

The key assumption is that the function class is unrestricted so that the values \(s(x)\) can be chosen independently at different inputs. If we have no restrictions on \(s\) then we can do this. After all, what is a function other than an assignment of \(s(x)\) to each \(x\)? If we can choose any function then we can choose each \(s(x)\) completely separately for each \(x\).



31.0.4 Question 4
We showed that \[
s^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{t}\mathbb{E}[\ell(Y,t)\mid X=x].
\] For squared-loss regression, this is \[
s^*(x)=\arg\min_t\mathbb E[(Y-t)^2\mid X=x].
\] Show that this is equivalent to: \[
s^*(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
\]


Answer

Expand the conditional objective: \[
\mathbb E[(Y-t)^2\mid X=x]
=\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X=x]-2t\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]+t^2.
\] Differentiate with respect to \(t\): \[
-2\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]+2t.
\] Setting this equal to zero gives \[
t=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] The second derivative is \(2>0\), so this critical point is the unique minimizer.



31.0.5 Question 5
At a particular input value \(x\), suppose the conditional distribution of \(Y\mid X=x\) assigns probability \(0.25\) to \(0\) and probability \(0.75\) to \(4\). Under squared loss, compute the optimal prediction \(s^*(x)\).


Answer

Under squared loss, \[
s^*(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] Here \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=0(0.25)+4(0.75)=3.
\] So the optimal prediction is \(s^*(x)=3\).



31.0.6 Question 6
Why is the exact-match estimator \[
\hat s(x)=\frac{1}{|\{n:X_n=x\}|}\sum_{n:X_n=x}Y_n
\] usually not useful when \(X\in\mathbb R^D\) has a continuous distribution? Make a probabilistic argument based on the fact that: \[
P(X=x)=0.
\]


Answer

If \(X\) has a continuous distribution, then for a fixed query point \(x\), \[
P(X=x)=0.
\] With finitely many training observations, the probability of observing many, or even any, exact matches \(X_n=x\) is usually zero (or negligible). So exact conditional averaging is not usable. Moreover, this woud only define predictions are points where we exactly have training data, but we want to be able to predict everywhere.



31.0.7 Question 7
Training inputs on the real line are \[
X_1=0,\quad X_2=1,\quad X_3=3,\quad X_4=4
\] with responses \[
Y_1=2,\quad Y_2=4,\quad Y_3=10,\quad Y_4=12.
\] Using Euclidean distance and query point \(x=2.6\), compute the KNN regression prediction for \(k=2\).


Answer

The distances from \(x=2.6\) are \[
|0-2.6|=2.6,\quad |1-2.6|=1.6,\quad |3-2.6|=0.4,\quad |4-2.6|=1.4.
\] The two nearest inputs are \(3\) and \(4\), with responses \(10\) and \(12\). Therefore \[
\hat s(2.6)=\frac{10+12}{2}=11.
\]



31.0.8 Question 8
For the same data as Question 7, compute the KNN regression prediction at \(x=2.6\) for \(k=4\). Compare it with the \(k=2\) prediction and state what changed.


Answer

For \(k=4\), all four responses are averaged: \[
\hat s(2.6)=\frac{2+4+10+12}{4}=7.
\] The \(k=2\) prediction was \(11\). Increasing \(k\) added farther-away points with smaller responses, so the prediction moved away from the local average near \(x=2.6\) and toward a more global average.



31.0.9 Question 9
In \(k\)-nearest neighbors regression, how does the choice of \(k\) affect the flexibility of the fitted curve?


Answer

Smaller values of \(k\) make the fitted curve more flexible. Each prediction is based on only a few nearby points, so the curve can respond strongly to local changes in the training data.
Larger values of \(k\) make the fitted curve less flexible. Each prediction averages over more points, which smooths out local variation and produces a more stable curve.
So, decreasing \(k\) increases flexibility, while increasing \(k\) decreases flexibility.



31.0.10 Question 10
Compare KNN regression and linear regression as estimators. Under squared loss, both methods target the conditional mean function \[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] State the main difference in how the two methods estimate it.


Answer

Linear regression estimates this target using a global parametric form, usually \(m(x)\approx w^\top x\). This imposes a single linear relationship across the feature space.
KNN estimates the target locally by averaging responses near the query point: \[
\hat s(x)=\frac1k\sum_{n\in\mathcal N_k(x)}Y_n.
\] It does not impose a global linear form, but its behavior depends strongly on local neighborhoods and the choice of distance.



31.0.11 Question 11
In KNN classification with classes \({1,\dots,C}\), show that minimizing 0-1 loss pointwise is equivalent to choosing the class with largest conditional probability \(P(Y=c\mid X=x)\).


Answer

In classification, the prediction is a class label. Suppose that at a fixed input value \(x\), we predict class \(c\).
Under 0-1 loss, the loss is
\[
\ell(Y,c)=\mathbf{1}\{Y\neq c\}.
\]
This loss is \(0\) if the prediction is correct and \(1\) if the prediction is incorrect.
The conditional risk at \(x\) is the expected loss given \(X=x\):
\[
L_x(c)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{Y\neq c\}\mid X=x].
\]
Because the expectation of an indicator is the probability of the event, this becomes
\[
L_x(c)=P(Y\neq c\mid X=x).
\]
So, for a fixed \(x\), minimizing the conditional 0-1 risk means choosing the class \(c\) that makes the probability of misclassification as small as possible.
Now use the fact that, if we predict class \(c\), the only way to be correct is for \(Y=c\). Therefore,
\[
P(Y\neq c\mid X=x)=1-P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]
Thus,
\[
L_x(c)=1-P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]
Since the \(1\) is the same for every possible class \(c\), minimizing \(L_x(c)\) is the same as maximizing \(P(Y=c\mid X=x)\).
Therefore, the pointwise optimal classifier is
\[
f^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{c} P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]
This is the Bayes classifier. It says that, at each input \(x\), the optimal prediction under 0-1 loss is the most likely class conditional on \(X=x\).



31.0.12 Question 12
For KNN classification, prove that the score \[
\hat s_c(x)=\frac1k\sum_{n\in\mathcal N_k(x)}\mathbf 1\{Y_n=c\}
\] is the fraction of neighbors whose class is \(c\).


Answer

Each indicator \(\mathbf 1\{Y_n=c\}\) equals \(1\) if neighbor \(n\) has class \(c\) and \(0\) otherwise. Summing over \(n\in\mathcal N_k(x)\) counts how many of the \(k\) neighbors have class \(c\). Dividing by \(k\) gives the fraction of neighbors in class \(c\).



31.0.13 Question 13
A KNN classifier uses \(k=7\). Among the seven nearest neighbors of a query point, the class labels are \[
A,A,B,A,C,B,A.
\] Compute \(\hat s_A(x)\), \(\hat s_B(x)\), and \(\hat s_C(x)\), and give the predicted class.


Answer

The counts are \(4\) for class \(A\), \(2\) for class \(B\), and \(1\) for class \(C\). Therefore \[
\hat s_A(x)=\frac47,
\qquad
\hat s_B(x)=\frac27,
\qquad
\hat s_C(x)=\frac17.
\] The largest score is \(\hat s_A(x)\), so the predicted class is \(A\).



31.0.14 Question 14
A student claims: “Scaling cannot change KNN predictions because scaling does not change the labels \(Y_n\).” Diagnose the flaw in this claim.


Answer

The flaw is that KNN predictions depend not only on labels but also on which points are selected as nearest neighbors. Scaling changes the distances between feature vectors, and therefore it can change the neighborhood set \(\mathcal N_k(x)\).
Even with the same labels \(Y_n\), a different neighbor set can produce a different average response in regression or a different majority vote in classification.



31.0.15 Question 15
For KNN regression, describe the qualitative behavior at the two extremes \(k=1\) and \(k=N\). Which one is more sensitive to individual training responses?


Answer

At \(k=1\), the prediction is the response of the single nearest training point. It is highly sensitive to individual training responses and can vary sharply as the nearest neighbor changes.
At \(k=N\), every prediction averages all training responses: \[
\hat s(x)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N Y_n.
\] This ignores the query location entirely because every point has the same neighbor set. Thus \(k=1\) is most sensitive to individual responses, while \(k=N\) ignores \(x\) the most.

title: 32  Bias-Variance Tradeoff - Review Questions
text:
This notebook contains review questions for lectures/080_bias_variance.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

32.0.1 Question 1
In the lecture’s setup, \(\hat f\) is random. Identify the source of this randomness and explain why \(f^*(x)\) is not random.


Answer

The fitted predictor \(\hat f= \hat f_{\mathcal D}\) is random because it is a function of the random training dataset \[
\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n.
\] Different draws of \(\mathcal D\) can produce different fitted functions and therefore different values \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)\).
At a fixed input \(x\), \(f^*(x)\) is the value of the true regression function at that input. The function \(f^*\) is treated as part of the data-generating distribution, not as something re-estimated from each sample. Thus \(f^*(x)\) is fixed in the pointwise decomposition.



32.0.2 Question 2
Starting from the model \(Y=f^*(X)+\varepsilon\), show that \[
(Y-\hat f(x))^2 = (f^*(x)-\hat f(x))^2+2\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f(x))+\varepsilon^2.
\]


Answer

At a fixed test input \(X=x\), the model gives \[
Y=f^*(x)+\varepsilon.
\] Therefore \[
(Y-\hat f(x))^2=(f^*(x)+\varepsilon-\hat f(x))^2.
\] Rearranging inside the square, \[
(f^*(x)-\hat f(x)+\varepsilon)^2
=(f^*(x)-\hat f(x))^2+2\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f(x))+\varepsilon^2.
\] These are the prediction-error term, the cross term, and the noise-squared term.



32.0.3 Question 3
Justify the step \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f(x))]=0.
\]


Answer

At test time, \(\varepsilon\) is the noise in the new response at \(X=x\), while \(\hat f(x)\) is determined by the training dataset \(\mathcal D\). The needed assumptions are that \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0
\] and that the test noise is independent of the training data, hence independent of \(\hat f(x)\).
Since \(f^*(x)\) is fixed and \(\hat f(x)\) is independent of \(\varepsilon\), \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f(x))]
=\mathbb E[\varepsilon]\mathbb E[f^*(x)-\hat f(x)]=0.
\]



32.0.4 Question 4
Distinguish the variance term \(\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f(x))\) from the noise variance \(\sigma^2\). What random quantity varies in each case?


Answer

The variance term \[
\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f(x))
\] measures how the fitted prediction at \(x\) changes across different random training datasets \(\mathcal D\).
The noise variance \[
\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X=x)
\] measures the randomness in the new response \(Y\) around the true signal \(f^*(x)\), even if the signal were known perfectly. The first is model instability; the second is irreducible output noise.



32.0.5 Question 5
Why is the noise term called irreducible error? Show that even if \(\hat f(x)=f^*(x)\) then \[
E[(Y-\hat f(x))^2 \mid X = x] = \sigma^2.
\]


Answer

If \(\hat f(x)=f^*(x)\) exactly, then squared prediction error at \(x\) is \[
(Y-\hat f(x))^2=(f^*(x)+\varepsilon-f^*(x))^2=\varepsilon^2.
\] Taking expectation gives \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2\mid X=x]=\sigma^2.
\] Thus even a perfect predictor of the true signal cannot remove the randomness in \(Y\) due to \(\varepsilon\). That is why \(\sigma^2\) is irreducible.



32.0.6 Question 6
A learning procedure has high bias but low variance at a point \(x\). Describe what repeated fitted models would look like at \(x\) relative to \(f^*(x)\).


Answer

Across repeated datasets, the fitted values \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)\) would be tightly clustered, because variance is low. However, the cluster would be centered far from \(f^*(x)\), because bias is high.
So the procedure is stable but systematically wrong at that point.



32.0.7 Question 7
At a fixed \(x\), suppose \[
\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f(x)]=2.5,
\qquad
f^*(x)=3.0,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f(x))=0.16,
\qquad
\sigma^2=0.09.
\] Compute the squared bias and \(R_f(x)\).


Answer

The bias is \[
2.5-3.0=-0.5,
\] so the squared bias is \[
(-0.5)^2=0.25.
\] The risk is \[
R_f(x)=0.25+0.16+0.09=0.50.
\]



32.0.8 Question 8
The lecture says flexible models are often low-bias and high-variance. State this claim in the context of KNN by comparing small \(k\) and large \(k\).


Answer

In KNN regression, small \(k\) uses very local averages. This makes the fitted function flexible, so it can adapt to local structure in \(f^*\) and often has lower bias. But it also depends strongly on a small number of training points, so it has higher variance across datasets.
Large \(k\) averages many points. This stabilizes predictions and lowers variance, but it can smooth over local structure and increase bias.



32.0.9 Question 9
Increasing sample size usually decreases variance while bias typically stays about the same. Explain why this statement assumes the model class or fitting rule is not fundamentally changed as \(n\) increases.


Answer

Variance measures sensitivity to the random training dataset. With more data, a fixed fitting rule usually becomes less sensitive to any particular sample, so variance tends to decrease.
Bias is determined largely by the systematic limitations of the model class or procedure. If the same kind of model is used as \(n\) grows, those approximation limitations may remain similar. But if the model class or tuning rule changes with \(n\), bias can change too. Thus the classical statement assumes the modeling procedure is held mostly fixed.



32.0.10 Question 10
Suppose \(\mathrm{Bias}_f(x)^2=0.36\), \(\mathrm{Var}_f(x)=0.04\), and \(\sigma^2=0.09\). If a richer model reduces squared bias to \(0.09\) but increases variance to \(0.20\), which model has lower pointwise risk at \(x\)?


Answer

The original model has risk \[
0.36+0.04+0.09=0.49.
\] The richer model has risk \[
0.09+0.20+0.09=0.38.
\] The richer model has lower pointwise risk at \(x\), despite its higher variance, because the reduction in squared bias is larger than the increase in variance.



32.0.11 Question 11
A student says: “Because variance is bad, we should always choose the lowest-variance model.” Diagnose the mistake using the decomposition from the lecture.


Answer

The mistake is ignoring squared bias. The pointwise risk is \[
R_f(x)=\mathrm{Bias}_f(x)^2+\mathrm{Var}_f(x)+\sigma^2.
\] A very low-variance model can still have high risk if its average prediction is far from \(f^*(x)\). The goal is not to minimize variance alone, but to balance squared bias and variance, since the noise term is not controlled by the model.



32.0.12 Question 12
Suppose the learning procedure always predicts \[
\hat f(x)=0
\] for every training dataset, while \[
f^*(x)=2.
\] Show that this procedure has zero variance but nonzero bias.


Answer

We then have: \[
\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f(x))=0
\] because the prediction never changes across datasets. But \[
\mathrm{Bias}_f(x)=\mathbb E[\hat f(x)]-f^*(x)=0-2=-2,
\] so the squared bias is \(4\).



32.0.13 Question 13
Does the bias-variance decomposition work exactly for the 0-1 loss? What about absolute error loss?


Answer

No. The derivation relies on expanding a square: \[
(Y-\hat f(x))^2.
\] This expansion produces terms that can be identified as squared bias, variance, and noise, with cross terms that vanish under the stated assumptions.
For other losses, such as absolute error or 0-1 loss, there is no analogous simple quadratic expansion into these exact three terms. The bias-variance idea may still be useful qualitatively, but the displayed formula is specific to squared-error regression.



32.0.14 Question 14
A model has pointwise risk \(R_f(x)=1.7\), squared bias \(0.8\), and variance \(0.6\). Under the lecture’s decomposition, what is \(\sigma^2\)?


Answer

Using \[
R_f(x)=\mathrm{Bias}_f(x)^2+\mathrm{Var}_f(x)+\sigma^2,
\] we get \[
\sigma^2=1.7-0.8-0.6=0.3.
\]



32.0.15 Question 15
At a point \(x\), three procedures have the following squared bias and variance, with common \(\sigma^2=0.1\):



procedure
squared bias
variance




A
0.50
0.05


B
0.20
0.20


C
0.05
0.60



Compute the risk for each procedure and identify the best one at this \(x\).


Answer

Procedure A has risk \[
0.50+0.05+0.10=0.65.
\] Procedure B has risk \[
0.20+0.20+0.10=0.50.
\] Procedure C has risk \[
0.05+0.60+0.10=0.75.
\] Procedure B is best at this \(x\) because it has the smallest total risk.



32.0.16 Question 16
A false proof says: “The cross term vanishes because \(\mathbb E[\hat f(x)-f^*(x)]=0\).” Identify why this proof is wrong in general.


Answer

The statement \[
\mathbb E[\hat f(x)-f^*(x)]=0
\] means the estimator is unbiased at \(x\). The lecture does not assume unbiasedness; in fact, bias may be nonzero and is one of the terms being measured.
The first cross term involving \(\varepsilon\) vanishes because the test noise has mean zero and is independent of \(\hat f(x)\). The second cross term in the bias-variance decomposition vanishes because \(\hat f(x)-\mathbb E[\hat f(x)]\) is centered, not because \(\hat f(x)-f^*(x)\) is centered.



32.0.17 Question 17
Suppose the irreducible noise variance is \(\sigma^2=1\). At a fixed test point \(x_0\), two prediction procedures have the following bias and variance:



Procedure
Bias\(^2\)
Variance




A
\(0\)
\(4\)


B
\(3\)
\(1\)



Using the bias-variance decomposition, show that the two procedures have the same overall risk at \(x_0\), but different bias-variance behavior.


Answer

For Procedure A, the risk is
\[
0+4+1=5.
\]
So Procedure A has total risk \(5\).
For Procedure B, the risk is
\[
3+1+1=5.
\]
So Procedure B also has total risk \(5\).
Therefore, the two procedures have the same overall risk at \(x_0\), even though the source of the error is different.

title: 33  Ridge Regression - Review Questions
text:
This notebook contains review questions for lectures/100_ridge.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

33.0.1 Question 1
The lecture describes ridge regression as an example of regularization. How does this regularization work for ridge, what quantity controls the strength of regularization, and what happens at the two extremes \(\lambda=0\) and \(\lambda\to\infty\).


Answer

Ridge regularizes the coefficient vector \(w\) by adding the penalty \[
\lambda\|w\|_2^2
\] to the squared-error training objective. The regularization strength is controlled by \(\lambda\ge0\).
At \(\lambda=0\), the penalty disappears and the problem reduces to OLS, assuming matching scaling conventions. As \(\lambda\to\infty\), any nonzero coefficient becomes extremely costly, so the fitted coefficients are driven toward \(0\).



33.0.2 Question 2
For \(w=(3,-4,12)\), compute \(\|w\|_2^2\). If \(\lambda=0.5\), what is the ridge penalty value \(\lambda\|w\|_2^2\)?


Answer

The squared norm is \[
\|w\|_2^2=3^2+(-4)^2+12^2=9+16+144=169.
\] Thus the penalty value is \[
\lambda\|w\|_2^2=0.5(169)=84.5.
\]



33.0.3 Question 3
Why does minimizing training error alone fail to control model complexity? How does ridge control model complexity?


Answer

Training error can be reduced by increasing flexibility, but greater flexibility can fit noise and sample-specific patterns. For example, in polynomial regression, increasing degree can keep lowering training error while eventually increasing test error. In KNN, very small \(k\) gives highly local fits that can have high variance.
Ridge addresses the same issue for linear regression by keeping the model class linear but penalizing large coefficients. The penalty discourages overly flexible or unstable coefficient choices even if they improve training error.



33.0.4 Question 4
Starting from the unnormalized ridge objective used in the solving section, \[
J(w)=\|y-Xw\|_2^2+\lambda\|w\|_2^2,
\] expand \(J(w)\) into quadratic form involving \(y^\top y\), \(w^\top X^\top y\), \(w^\top X^\top Xw\), and \(w^\top w\).


Answer

First, \[
\|y-Xw\|_2^2=(y-Xw)^\top(y-Xw).
\] Expanding gives \[
y^\top y-y^\top Xw-w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw.
\] Since \(y^\top Xw\) is a scalar equal to \(w^\top X^\top y\), this becomes \[
y^\top y-2w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw.
\] Adding the penalty gives \[
J(w)=y^\top y-2w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw+
\lambda w^\top w.
\]



33.0.5 Question 5
Differentiate the expanded objective from Question 4 and derive the ridge normal equations.


Answer

Using the standard rules, \[
\nabla_w(y^\top y)=0,
\qquad
\nabla_w(w^\top X^\top y)=X^\top y,
\] \[
\nabla_w(w^\top X^\top Xw)=2X^\top Xw,
\qquad
\nabla_w(w^\top w)=2w.
\] Therefore \[
\nabla_wJ(w)=2X^\top Xw-2X^\top y+2\lambda w.
\] Setting this equal to zero and dividing by \(2\) gives \[
X^\top Xw-X^\top y+
\lambda w=0.
\] Thus \[
(X^\top X+
\lambda I)w=X^\top y.
\]



33.0.6 Question 7
In the scalar case \(D=1\), let \(X^\top X=9\), \(X^\top y=18\), and \(\lambda=3\) under the unnormalized convention. Compute the OLS coefficient and the ridge coefficient.


Answer

The OLS coefficient is \[
\hat w_{OLS}=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y=\frac{18}{9}=2.
\] The ridge coefficient is \[
\hat w_\lambda=(X^\top X+
\lambda)^{-1}X^\top y=\frac{18}{9+3}=\frac{18}{12}=1.5.
\] Ridge shrinks the coefficient toward zero.



33.0.7 Question 8
Why does ridge regression stabilize solutions when features are highly correlated? Give a precise explanation using the lecture’s example where \(x_2\approx x_1\).


Answer

If \(x_2\approx x_1\), then \[
w_1x_1+w_2x_2\approx (w_1+w_2)x_1.
\] Many pairs \((w_1,w_2)\) with similar sums can produce nearly the same predictions. OLS may therefore choose large cancelling coefficients, such as \((100,-99)\), with little change in training error.
Ridge penalizes \[
w_1^2+w_2^2,
\] so large cancelling coefficients become costly. Among coefficient vectors with similar fit, ridge prefers smaller Euclidean norm, producing a more stable solution.



33.0.8 Question 9
Suppose \(X^\top Xv=\sigma^2v\) for a nonzero vector \(v\). Show that \(v\) is also an eigenvector of \(X^\top X+
\lambda I\), and identify its new eigenvalue.


Answer

Compute \[
(X^\top X+
\lambda I)v=X^\top Xv+
\lambda Iv.
\] Using \(X^\top Xv=\sigma^2v\) and \(Iv=v\), \[
(X^\top X+
\lambda I)v=\sigma^2v+
\lambda v=(\sigma^2+
\lambda)v.
\] Thus \(v\) remains an eigenvector, and the new eigenvalue is \(\sigma^2+
\lambda\).



33.0.9 Question 10
Let the smallest and largest eigenvalues of \(X^\top X\) be \(a\) and \(b\), with \(0\le a\le b\). Then for \(\lambda>0\), the condition number of \(X^\top X\) is \(a/b\) and the condition number of \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) is \((a+\lambda)/(b+\lambda)\). Show that \[
\frac{b+
\lambda}{a+
\lambda}\le \frac{b}{a}
\] when \(a>0\) which shows that ridge improves conditioning.


Answer

Assume \(a>0\). Since all quantities are positive, cross-multiply: \[
\frac{b+
\lambda}{a+
\lambda}\le \frac{b}{a}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a(b+
\lambda)
\le b(a+
\lambda).
\] Expanding, \[
ab+a\lambda\le ab+b\lambda.
\] Cancel \(ab\): \[
a\lambda\le b\lambda,
\] which is true because \(a\le b\) and \(\lambda>0\). Thus ridge decreases the condition number unless \(a=b\). This means the linear system is better conditioned and typically more stable.



33.0.10 Question 11
Suppose \(X^\top X\) has eigenvalues \(0\), \(2\), and \(10\). For \(\lambda=1\), list the eigenvalues of \(X^\top X+
\lambda I\) and compute its condition number.


Answer

Adding \(\lambda I\) shifts every eigenvalue by \(1\). The new eigenvalues are \[
1,
\quad 3,
\quad 11.
\] The condition number is \[
K=\frac{11}{1}=11.
\] The original matrix was singular because it had a zero eigenvalue, but the ridge matrix is invertible.



33.0.11 Question 12
For orthonormal predictors satisfying \(X^\top X=I\), derive the ridge estimator and express it in terms of the OLS estimator.


Answer

The ridge estimator is \[
\hat w_\lambda=(X^\top X+
\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.
\] Using \(X^\top X=I\), \[
\hat w_\lambda=(I+
\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y=((1+
\lambda)I)^{-1}X^\top y.
\] Therefore \[
\hat w_\lambda=\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}X^\top y.
\] Since \(\hat w_{OLS}=X^\top y\) in this case, \[
\hat w_\lambda=\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}\hat w_{OLS}.
\]



33.0.12 Question 13
In an orthonormal-design problem, suppose \(\hat w_{OLS}=(4,-2,1)\) and \(\lambda=3\). Compute \(\hat w_\lambda\).


Answer

The shrinkage factor is \[
\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}=\frac14.
\] Therefore \[
\hat w_\lambda=\frac14(4,-2,1)=\left(1,-\frac12,\frac14\right).
\]



33.0.13 Question 14
The lecture recommends standardizing predictors before ridge regression. Why is this necessary for the penalty \(\lambda\sum_jw_j^2\) to treat predictors comparably?


Answer

Coefficient size depends on feature units. If one predictor is measured in thousands and another in units near one, the same predictive effect can require very different coefficient magnitudes. Since ridge penalizes coefficient magnitudes directly, \[
\lambda\sum_jw_j^2,
\] the penalty depends on the measurement scale of each feature.
Standardizing features to comparable scales, usually mean zero and variance one, makes coefficient sizes more comparable. Then the penalty is less distorted by arbitrary units.



33.0.14 Question 15
State the penalized and constrained forms of ridge regression.


Answer

The penalized form is \[
\min_w \hat R(w)+
\lambda\|w\|_2^2.
\] The constrained form is \[
\min_w \hat R(w)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \|w\|_2^2\le t.
\]



33.0.15 Question 16
For a diagonal design with \[
X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
X^\top y=\begin{pmatrix}8\\3\end{pmatrix},
\] compute the ridge solution for \(\lambda=1\).


Answer

The ridge system is \[
(X^\top X+
\lambda I)w=X^\top y.
\] With \(\lambda=1\), \[
X^\top X+
I=
\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\] Therefore \[
w=\begin{pmatrix}5^{-1}&0\\0&2^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}8\\3\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}8/5\\3/2\end{pmatrix}.
\] So \[
\hat w_\lambda=(1.6,1.5)^\top.
\]



33.0.16 Question 17
How does increasing \(\lambda\) affect the bias-variance tradeoff in ridge regression? Give the expected direction of training error and test error for very small versus moderate \(\lambda\).


Answer

Increasing \(\lambda\) shrinks coefficients and reduces model flexibility. This usually increases bias but lowers variance.
For very small \(\lambda\), ridge is close to OLS: training error is low, but variance may be high and test error can be poor in noisy, collinear, or high-dimensional settings. For moderate \(\lambda\), training error may increase, but test error can decrease because the reduction in variance and instability outweighs the increase in bias. For very large \(\lambda\), underfitting can make test error increase again.



33.0.17 Question 18
The lecture says ridge can handle \(D>N\) even though OLS may not have a unique solution. Give a precise explanation.


Answer

When \(D>N\), the columns of \(X\) are often linearly dependent, so \(X^\top X\) is singular and the OLS normal equations may not determine a unique coefficient vector.
For any \(\lambda>0\), ridge uses \[
X^\top X+
\lambda I,
\] whose eigenvalues are shifted upward by \(\lambda\). This matrix is invertible, so ridge has a unique solution.

title: 34  LASSO - Review Questions
text:
This notebook contains review questions for lectures/110_lasso.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

34.0.1 Question 1
LASSO stands for least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. Why?


Answer

The penalty \[
\lambda\|w\|_1=\lambda\sum_j |w_j|
\] causes shrinkage because it makes large coefficient magnitudes costly, pulling estimates toward zero.
Selection occurs because the \(\ell_1\) penalty can set some coefficients exactly equal to zero. A coefficient with \(\hat w_j=0\) effectively removes predictor \(j\) from the fitted linear model. This selects out the corresponding variable.



34.0.2 Question 2
For \(w=(3,-1,0,2)\), compute \(\|w\|_1\), \(\|w\|_2^2\), and the number of “selected” variables.


Answer

The \(\ell_1\) norm is \[
\|w\|_1=|3|+|-1|+|0|+|2|=6.
\] The squared \(\ell_2\) norm is \[
\|w\|_2^2=3^2+(-1)^2+0^2+2^2=14.
\] There are three nonzero coefficients, so the number of selected variables is \(3\).



34.0.3 Question 3
What is the main optimization hurdle for LASSO as compared to ridge?


Answer

Ridge uses the smooth squared \(\ell_2\) penalty \(\|w\|_2^2\), so the objective is differentiable and leads to normal equations with a closed-form matrix solution.
LASSO uses the \(\ell_1\) penalty \(\|w\|_1=\sum_j |w_j|\). The absolute value is not differentiable at zero, so the objective is convex but nonsmooth. Because of this nonsmoothness, LASSO generally does not have a simple closed-form matrix formula like ridge.



34.0.4 Question 4
State the subdifferential of \(|u|\) at \(u>0\), \(u=0\), and \(u<0\).


Answer

The subdifferential is \[
\partial |u|=\begin{cases}
\{1\},&u>0,\\
[-1,1],&u=0,\\
\{-1\},&u<0.
\end{cases}
\] At zero, the subdifferential is an entire interval rather than a single slope.



34.0.5 Question 5
In coordinate descent, the partial residual for coordinate \(j\) is \[
r_j=y-\sum_{k\ne j}x_kw_k.
\] Show that if \(\hat y=Xw=\sum_k x_kw_k\), then \[
r_j=y-\hat y+x_jw_j.
\]


Answer

Since \[
\hat y=\sum_k x_kw_k=x_jw_j+\sum_{k\ne j}x_kw_k,
\] we have \[
\sum_{k\ne j}x_kw_k=\hat y-x_jw_j.
\] Substitute into the definition of \(r_j\): \[
r_j=y-(\hat y-x_jw_j)=y-\hat y+x_jw_j.
\]



34.0.6 Question 6
In the coordinate-descent derivation, \(c_j=(1/N)x_j^\top r_j\). Give an interpretation of \(c_j\).


Answer

The value \[
c_j=\frac1N x_j^\top r_j
\] measures the empirical alignment, or correlation up to scaling, between feature \(j\) and the remaining residual. If \(|c_j|\) is large, feature \(j\) explains residual variation not already explained by the other variables.



34.0.7 Question 7
Starting from \[
\frac{1}{2N}\|r_j-x_jw_j\|_2^2+
\lambda|w_j|,
\] expand the terms that depend on \(w_j\) and derive \[
g(w_j)=\frac12a_jw_j^2-c_jw_j+
\lambda|w_j|,
\] where \(a_j=(1/N)x_j^\top x_j\) and \(c_j=(1/N)x_j^\top r_j\). You can drop any term that doesn’t depend on \(w_j\).


Answer

Expand the squared term: \[
\frac{1}{2N}(r_j-x_jw_j)^\top(r_j-x_jw_j)
=
\frac{1}{2N}\left(r_j^\top r_j-2w_jx_j^\top r_j+w_j^2x_j^\top x_j\right).
\] The term \((1/(2N))r_j^\top r_j\) does not depend on \(w_j\), so it can be dropped for minimization. The remaining terms are \[
-\frac1N w_jx_j^\top r_j+
\frac12\frac1N x_j^\top x_j w_j^2+
\lambda|w_j|.
\] Using \(a_j=(1/N)x_j^\top x_j\) and \(c_j=(1/N)x_j^\top r_j\) gives \[
g(w_j)=\frac12a_jw_j^2-c_jw_j+
\lambda|w_j|.
\]



34.0.8 Question 8
For the coordinate objective \[
g(w_j)=\frac12a_jw_j^2-c_jw_j+
\lambda|w_j|,
\] derive the subdifferential.


Answer

The differentiable part is \[
\frac12a_jw_j^2-c_jw_j,
\] whose derivative is \[
a_jw_j-c_j.
\] The nonsmooth part is \(\lambda|w_j|\), whose subdifferential is \[
\lambda\partial|w_j|.
\] Adding the derivative of the smooth part and the subdifferential of the nonsmooth part gives \[
\partial g(w_j)=a_jw_j-c_j+
\lambda\partial|w_j|.
\]



34.0.9 Question 9
At \(w_j=0\), show that \[
\partial g(0)=[-c_j-\lambda,
-c_j+
\lambda].
\] Then state the condition on \(c_j\) under which \(w_j=0\) satisfies the optimality condition.


Answer

At \(w_j=0\), \[
a_jw_j-c_j=-c_j.
\] Also, \[
\partial|0|=[-1,1].
\] Therefore \[
\partial g(0)=-c_j+
\lambda[-1,1]=[-c_j-
\lambda,-c_j+
\lambda].
\] The optimality condition is \(0\in\partial g(0)\). This holds exactly when \[
-c_j-
\lambda\le0\le -c_j+
\lambda,
\] which is equivalent to \[
|c_j|\le\lambda.
\]



34.0.10 Question 10
Derive the positive-coordinate case of the LASSO update: if \(c_j>\lambda\), show that the minimizer satisfies
\[
w_j=\frac{c_j-\lambda}{a_j}.
\]


Answer

The coordinate-wise objective has subdifferential
\[
\partial g(w_j)=a_jw_j-c_j+\lambda \partial |w_j|.
\]
A value of \(w_j\) is optimal exactly when
\[
0 \in \partial g(w_j).
\]
Assume \(c_j>\lambda\). First check whether \(w_j=0\) can be optimal. At \(w_j=0\),
\[
\partial g(0)=[-c_j-\lambda,,-c_j+\lambda].
\]
Since \(c_j>\lambda\), the upper endpoint satisfies \(-c_j+\lambda<0\). Therefore this whole interval is negative, so \(0\notin\partial g(0)\). Thus \(w_j=0\) is not optimal.
Now check whether a negative value can be optimal. If \(w_j<0\), then \(\partial |w_j|={-1}\), so
\[
\partial g(w_j)={a_jw_j-c_j-\lambda}.
\]
Since \(a_j>0\) and \(w_j<0\), we have \(a_jw_j<0\). Also, \(c_j>\lambda>0\). Therefore \(a_jw_j-c_j-\lambda<0\), so the subdifferential cannot contain zero for any \(w_j<0\).
So the minimizer must be positive. For \(w_j>0\), \(\partial |w_j|={1}\), so
\[
\partial g(w_j)={a_jw_j-c_j+\lambda}.
\]
To make zero belong to this set, solve
\[
a_jw_j-c_j+\lambda=0.
\]
This gives
\[
w_j=\frac{c_j-\lambda}{a_j}.
\]
Because \(c_j>\lambda\) and \(a_j>0\), this value is positive. Therefore it is consistent with the positive case and satisfies the subgradient optimality condition. Since \(g\) is convex, it is the minimizer.



34.0.11 Question 11
Compute \(S(c,\lambda)\) for \(\lambda=0.5\) and \[
c\in\{-1.2,-0.5,-0.1,0.7,2.0\}.
\]


Answer

Using soft-thresholding:

\(S(-1.2,0.5)=-1.2+0.5=-0.7\).
\(S(-0.5,0.5)=0\) because \(|c|\le\lambda\).
\(S(-0.1,0.5)=0\) because \(|c|\le\lambda\).
\(S(0.7,0.5)=0.7-0.5=0.2\).
\(S(2.0,0.5)=2.0-0.5=1.5\).




34.0.12 Question 12
A coordinate has \(a_j=2\), \(c_j=-3\), and \(\lambda=1\). Compute the coordinate descent update for \(w_j\).


Answer

Since \[
c_j=-3<-
\lambda=-1,
\] use the negative case: \[
w_j\leftarrow\frac{c_j+
\lambda}{a_j}=\frac{-3+1}{2}=-1.
\]



34.0.13 Question 13
Compare ridge and LASSO in the orthonormal-predictor case. If \(z_j\) is the OLS coefficient, what does ridge do to \(z_j\), and what does LASSO do to \(z_j\)?


Answer

In the orthonormal case, ridge rescales every coefficient by the same factor: \[
\hat w^{ridge}_j=\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}z_j
\] under the lecture’s ridge convention.
LASSO applies soft-thresholding: \[
\hat w^{lasso}_j=S(z_j,\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}(z_j)(|z_j|-
\lambda)_+.
\] Thus ridge continuously shrinks all coefficients, while LASSO sets coefficients to zero when \(|z_j|\le\lambda\) and shrinks the rest by subtracting \(\lambda\) from their magnitude.



34.0.14 Question 14
For orthonormal predictors, let \(z=(2.0,0.4,-1.5)\) and \(\lambda=1\). Compute the LASSO solution and the ridge solution using the shrinkage factor \(1/(1+
\lambda)\).


Answer

For LASSO, \[
S(2.0,1)=1.0,
\qquad
S(0.4,1)=0,
\qquad
S(-1.5,1)=-0.5.
\] So \[
\hat w^{lasso}=(1.0,0,-0.5).
\] For ridge, the shrinkage factor is \[
\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}=\frac12.
\] Thus \[
\hat w^{ridge}=(1.0,0.2,-0.75).
\]



34.0.15 Question 15
In two dimensions, describe the set \[
\{(w_1,w_2): |w_1|+|w_2|\le 1\}.
\] List its four vertices.


Answer

The set is the two-dimensional \(\ell_1\) unit ball, which is a diamond. Its boundary consists of the lines \[
|w_1|+|w_2|=1.
\] The four vertices are \[
(1,0),
\quad
(0,1),
\quad
(-1,0),
\quad
(0,-1).
\] These vertices lie on the coordinate axes.



34.0.16 Question 16
Use the geometry from the lecture to explain why LASSO can produce exact zeros while ridge usually does not.


Answer

In the constrained view, ridge uses a round \(\ell_2\) ball, while LASSO uses a diamond-shaped \(\ell_1\) ball. The LASSO diamond has corners on the coordinate axes.
The solution is where the smallest attainable loss contour touches the constraint region. Because the \(\ell_1\) ball has corners on the axes, tangency often occurs at a point where one or more coordinates are exactly zero. The ridge ball is smooth and round, so tangency is less likely to occur exactly on an axis; ridge usually shrinks coefficients without setting them exactly to zero.



34.0.17 Question 17
For coefficient vectors \(u=(1,1)\) and \(v=(2,0)\), compare their \(\ell_1\) and squared \(\ell_2\) penalties. Use this to explain why LASSO may be indifferent between spreading and concentrating coefficients in some correlated-feature settings.


Answer

For \(u=(1,1)\), \[
\|u\|_1=2,
\qquad
\|u\|_2^2=1^2+1^2=2.
\] For \(v=(2,0)\), \[
\|v\|_1=2,
\qquad
\|v\|_2^2=2^2+0^2=4.
\] The two vectors have the same \(\ell_1\) norm but different squared \(\ell_2\) norms. This shows that an \(\ell_1\) penalty may not strongly prefer spreading weight across correlated variables, while ridge’s squared \(\ell_2\) penalty favors spreading because it penalizes concentration more heavily.



34.0.18 Question 18
Describe the qualitative relationship between \(\lambda\) and selected model complexity.


Answer

As \(\lambda\) increases, the number of nonzero coefficients decreases. Larger \(\lambda\) imposes stronger \(\ell_1\) regularization, so more coefficients fail the soft-thresholding condition and become zero.
Thus selected model complexity, measured by the number of nonzero coefficients, decreases as \(\lambda\) increases.



34.0.19 Question 19
Why should predictors be standardized before applying LASSO?


Answer

LASSO penalizes coefficient magnitudes through \[
\lambda\sum_j |w_j|.
\] Coefficient magnitude depends on feature units. If one predictor is measured in thousands, a small coefficient can have a large predictive effect. If another predictor is measured in tiny units, the same predictive effect may require a large coefficient.
Without standardization, LASSO may penalize the small-scale variable more heavily simply because its coefficient must be numerically larger. Standardizing puts predictors on comparable scales so the penalty treats them more fairly.

title: 35  Elastic Net and Penalized Logistic Regression - Review Questions
text:
35.0.1 Question 1
In the elastic net objective \[
\frac{1}{2N}\|y-Xw\|_2^2+\lambda\left(\rho\|w\|_1+\frac{1-\rho}{2}\|w\|_2^2\right),
\] state the role of \(\lambda\) and the role of \(\rho\). What happens at \(\rho=0\) and \(\rho=1\)?


Answer

The parameter \(\lambda\ge0\) controls the overall strength of regularization. Larger \(\lambda\) places more weight on the penalty relative to the squared-error fit term.
The parameter \(\rho\in[0,1]\) controls the mix between the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) parts. At \(\rho=1\), the penalty is purely \(\ell_1\), giving LASSO. At \(\rho=0\), the penalty is purely squared \(\ell_2\), giving ridge up to constant scaling of \(\lambda\).



35.0.2 Question 2
For \(w=(2,-1,0)\), \(\lambda=3\), and \(\rho=0.4\), compute the elastic net penalty term \[
\lambda\left(\rho\|w\|_1+\frac{1-\rho}{2}\|w\|_2^2\right).
\]


Answer

First, \[
\|w\|_1=|2|+|-1|+0=3,
\] and \[
\|w\|_2^2=2^2+(-1)^2+0^2=5.
\] Thus the unscaled mixed penalty is \[
0.4(3)+\frac{1-0.4}{2}(5)=1.2+0.3(5)=1.2+1.5=2.7.
\] Multiplying by \(\lambda=3\) gives \[
3(2.7)=8.1.
\]



35.0.3 Question 3
Why does the lecture say elastic net is especially useful when predictors are strongly correlated? Compare the expected coefficient behavior of ridge, LASSO, and elastic net in a correlated signal group.


Answer

Ridge tends to spread weight across correlated predictors because its \(\ell_2\) penalty stabilizes large coefficient swings but does not create exact zeros. LASSO encourages sparsity, so in a correlated group it may select one representative variable and set the others to zero, which can make selected variables unstable.
Elastic net combines these behaviors. Its \(\ell_1\) part can remove irrelevant variables, while its \(\ell_2\) part encourages stability and can keep several variables from a correlated signal group instead of forcing a single representative.



35.0.4 Question 4
The lecture’s coordinate update is \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{S(z_j,\lambda\rho)}{a_j+\lambda(1-\rho)}.
\] Show explicitly that this reduces to the LASSO update when \(\rho=1\) and to a ridge-like update when \(\rho=0\).


Answer

If \(\rho=1\), then the threshold is \(\lambda\rho=\lambda\) and the denominator is \[
a_j+\lambda(1-1)=a_j.
\] Thus \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{S(z_j,\lambda)}{a_j},
\] which is the LASSO coordinate update.
If \(\rho=0\), then the threshold is \(0\), so \(S(z_j,0)=z_j\), and the denominator is \[
a_j+\lambda.
\] Thus \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{z_j}{a_j+\lambda},
\] which is ridge-like shrinkage.



35.0.5 Question 5
For intermediate \(0<\rho<1\), why does elastic net both threshold and shrink? Use the coordinate update formula in your answer.


Answer

The numerator \[
S(z_j,\lambda\rho)
\] soft-thresholds \(z_j\). If \(|z_j|\le\lambda\rho\), the numerator is zero, so the coefficient is set exactly to zero. This is the LASSO-like thresholding effect.
When \(|z_j|>\lambda\rho\), the numerator is nonzero but has reduced magnitude. Then the denominator \[
a_j+\lambda(1-\rho)
\] further shrinks the coefficient. This is the ridge-like stabilization effect.



35.0.6 Question 6
Assume standardized predictors so \(a_j=1\). Let \(z_j=2.5\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(\rho=0.5\). Compute the elastic net coordinate update.


Answer

The threshold is \[
\lambda\rho=1(0.5)=0.5.
\] Since \(z_j=2.5>0.5\), \[
S(2.5,0.5)=2.5-0.5=2.0.
\] The denominator is \[
a_j+\lambda(1-\rho)=1+1(0.5)=1.5.
\] Thus \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{2.0}{1.5}=\frac43.
\]



35.0.7 Question 7
Suppose \(z_j=0.3\), \(a_j=1\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(\rho=0.5\). Compute the elastic net coordinate update.


Answer

The threshold is \[
\lambda\rho=0.5.
\] Since \(|z_j|=0.3\le0.5\), \[
S(z_j,0.5)=0.
\] Therefore \[
w_j\leftarrow \frac{0}{1+1(1-0.5)}=0.
\] The coordinate signal is not strong enough to overcome the \(\ell_1\) part of the penalty, so the coefficient is set to zero.



35.0.8 Question 8
The lecture says different books and software use different constants in front of the squared-error and ridge terms. Explain why multiplying the whole penalty by a constant often only changes the scale of \(\lambda\) rather than the statistical idea.


Answer

Suppose an objective contains \[
\lambda c\,\Omega(w)
\] for some positive constant \(c\). If we define a new tuning parameter \[
\lambda'=c\lambda,
\] then the penalty becomes \[
\lambda'\Omega(w).
\] Thus changing constants can often be absorbed by changing the numerical value of \(\lambda\). The path is parameterized differently, but the basic fit-complexity tradeoff is the same.



35.0.9 Question 9
Why does tuning elastic net generally require a two-dimensional grid search, while ridge and LASSO each require only a one-dimensional penalty search in the lecture’s setup?


Answer

Ridge and LASSO each have one main penalty-strength parameter, \(\lambda\), after the penalty type is fixed. Elastic net has both the overall strength \(\lambda\) and the mixing parameter \(\rho\).
The value of \(\lambda\) controls how much regularization is applied, while \(\rho\) controls the balance between \(\ell_1\) sparsity and \(\ell_2\) stabilization. Both affect the fitted model, so cross-validation typically searches over pairs \((\lambda,\rho)\).



35.0.10 Question 10
Why is the intercept \(w_0\) usually not penalized in penalized logistic regression, according to the same logic used for ridge and LASSO?


Answer

The intercept controls the baseline log-odds, or baseline class probability, before feature effects are applied. It is not a measure of model complexity in the same way that feature coefficients are.
Penalizing \(w_0\) would artificially shrink the baseline probability toward a default value, potentially introducing unnecessary bias. Therefore the penalty is usually applied only to \(w\), not to \(w_0\).



35.0.11 Question 11
In sklearn, suppose two logistic models differ only in C: one has C=0.01 and one has C=100. Which one is more strongly regularized? Which one would you expect to have more nonzero coefficients under an elastic net penalty with fixed l1_ratio?


Answer

C is inverse regularization strength, so smaller C means stronger regularization. Thus C=0.01 is more strongly regularized than C=100.
With fixed l1_ratio, the model with C=100 has weaker regularization, so more coefficients can enter the model. The model with C=0.01 is expected to have fewer nonzero coefficients.



35.0.12 Question 12
Map the sklearn parameter l1_ratio to the lecture’s penalty mix. What do l1_ratio=0, l1_ratio=1, and l1_ratio=0.5 mean?


Answer

l1_ratio plays the role of the elastic net mixing parameter \(\rho\).

l1_ratio=0 means \(\rho=0\), giving a purely ridge-like logistic penalty.
l1_ratio=1 means \(\rho=1\), giving a purely LASSO logistic penalty.
l1_ratio=0.5 gives an elastic net penalty with both \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) components.




35.0.13 Question 13
For an elastic net logistic path with fixed l1_ratio=0.5, suppose the nonzero counts at \(C=0.01,0.1,1,10\) are \(2,8,18,30\). Interpret the trend in terms of regularization strength.


Answer

As \(C\) increases, regularization weakens because \(C\) is inverse regularization strength. With weaker regularization, more coefficients are allowed to enter the model.
The nonzero counts increasing from \(2\) to \(30\) are therefore consistent with the lecture’s statement that larger \(C\) allows larger and more numerous coefficients.
